keyVerseText: The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God.
rootMeaning: The root of שָׁכֵחַ (shâkêach) is שָׁכַח (shâkach), which conveys the idea of forgetting or causing to forget, often implying a lapse of memory or attention. This root carries nuances beyond the simple English term 'forget,' suggesting not only the act of failing to recall but also a potential cessation of care or regard. Thus, the root sense encompasses both the cognitive failure to remember and a relational or moral disengagement, enriching the understanding of שָׁכֵחַ as more than mere forgetfulness.
usageInScripture: The word שָׁכֵחַ appears twice in Scripture and is consistently translated as 'that forget,' indicating a clear and focused semantic range. It is used adjectivally to describe those who are forgetful, particularly in relation to God, as seen in the example of nations that forget Him. This consistency highlights the word's thematic emphasis on spiritual forgetfulness or neglect rather than mere absentmindedness, underscoring a moral and covenantal dimension in its biblical usage.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding שָׁכֵחַ in its original sense deepens our awareness of the spiritual peril in forgetting God. It is not simply a mental lapse but a willful or careless turning away from the holiness and covenant relationship with Him. This forgetfulness leads to moral decay and judgment, as the Scriptures warn. For the Christian faith, this term reminds believers of the vital importance of continual remembrance and devotion to God, who is faithful even when His people are forgetful. Christ’s work restores and renews this memory and relationship, calling His followers to faithful remembrance and obedience.
keyVerseReflection: Psalm 9:17 states, 'The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God.' The use of שָׁכֵחַ here powerfully conveys that the nations’ downfall is linked to their spiritual forgetfulness—an active neglect of God’s presence and holiness. This forgetfulness is not innocent but brings about judgment, showing the serious consequences of turning away from God. The verse thus serves as a sober warning and a call to remember and honor God continually.
